sudan.summary: تتفاقم معاناة عشرات آلاف النازحين السودانيين في مدينتي الأبيض والدمازين بسبب استمرار المواجهات بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع. يعاني النازحون من نقص حاد في الغذاء ووسائل الإيواء، خاصة مع اقتراب فصل الشتاء. تشير التقارير إلى أن مئات الأسر تفترش الأرض في مخيمات مدينة الأبيض، حيث تنتظر المساعدات الإنسانية التي تأخرت. كما حذرت منظمة الأمم المتحدة للأغذية والزراعة (الفاو) من أن السودان أصبح واحداً من أكبر بؤر الجوع في العالم. في النيل الأزرق، يواجه مئات الآلاف من النازحين ظروفاً قاسية، حيث فروا من هجمات قوات الدعم السريع، مما أدى إلى نزوح سكان 35 قرية نحو مدينة الدمازين. الوضع الإنساني يتدهور بسرعة، مما يستدعي استجابة عاجلة من المنظمات الإنسانية لتلبية احتياجات هؤلاء النازحين.

درمان خلال أسبوع واحد، وسط نقص الرعاية الطبية والغذاء داخل السجن، وحذرت من تدهور الأوضاع الإنسانية والصحية داخل السجن المعروف بـ”دار التائبات”. ويأتي ذلك في ظل استمرار الحرب في السودان منذ أبريل 2023، وما صاحبها من تدهور في الخدمات الصحية والأوضاع الإنسانية، وتزايد الضغوط على المؤسسات ومرافق الاحتجاز، وسط دعوات حقوقية متكررة لضمان سلامة المحتجزين وحماية حقوقهم الأساسية. وتتطلب المعايير الدولية ضرورة توفير الرعاية الصحية والغذاء والمياه والنظافة للمحتجزين، وحظر المعاملة القاسية أو المهينة، كما تدعو إلى عدم سجن الأشخاص لمجرد العجز عن الوفاء بالتزامات مالية مدنية. وأعربت الشبكة، في بيان، عن قلقها إزاء وفاة النزيلة سهيلة عبد الكريم داخل السجن، في ظروف تشير إلى احتمال ارتباط الوفاة بالإهمال الطبي وغياب الرعاية الصحية والتغذية الكافية. وأشارت الشبكة السودانية لحقوق الإنسان إلى أن الضحية أودعت السجن على خلفية تعثرها في سداد التزام مالي. وأضافت أن تقارير تلقتها أفادت بوفاة ست نزيلات أخريات خلال الأسبوع ذاته، ما يرفع عدد الوفيات المبلغ عنها إلى سبع حالات، وطالبت بفتح تحقيق مستقل وعاجل لتحديد أسباب الوفاة والملابسات المحيطة بها، ومحاسبة المسؤولين عن أي تقصير. وأكدت الشبكة أن احتجاز النساء بسبب العجز عن سداد الديون المدنية يثير إشكالات قانونية وحقوقية، داعية إلى الإفراج عن المحتجزات في هذه القضايا أو اتخاذ تدابير بديلة لا تسلب الحرية، مع مراعاة حقوق الأطراف المعنية. وشددت الشبكة على ضرورة مراجعة القوانين والممارسات المتعلقة بالحبس في قضايا الديون المدنية، وإنهاء الممارسات التي تؤدي إلى سلب الحرية بسبب الفقر أو العجز المالي، وحملت السلطات والجهات المسؤولة عن إدارة السجون مسؤولية حماية حياة المحتجزات وضمان الرعاية الصحية والمعاملة الإنسانية. وطالبت بتشكيل لجنة تحقيق مستقلة للتحقيق في الوفيات، وإجراء تقييم عاجل للأوضاع الصحية داخل السجن، وتوفير الأدوية والغذاء ومياه الشرب النظيفة، وإجراء فحوص طبية لجميع النزيلات، ونقل الحالات الحرجة إلى المستشفيات دون تأخير. كما دعت إلى السماح للمنظمات الحقوقية والإنسانية والجهات الطبية المستقلة بزيارة السجون ومراكز الاحتجاز، والاطلاع على أوضاع المحتجزات، وضمان التواصل المنتظم مع أسرهن ومحاميهن، وإبلاغ ذوي النزيلات بأي تدهور صحي أو وفاة. يذكر أن الشبكة السودانية لحقوق الإنسان منظمة حقوقية تُعنى برصد وتوثيق انتهاكات حقوق الإنسان بالسودان والدفاع عن الحقوق والحريات الأساسية وتسليط الضوء على الانتهاكات ومساءلة الجهات المسؤولة عنها. – فاقمت المعارك في إقليمي النيل الأزرق وكردفان تدفقات النازحين الجدد إلى كل من الدمازين والأبيض، في حين وصل الآلاف منهم إلى دولة جنوب السودان. وتزايدت وتيرة المعارك في كردفان والنيل الأزرق على إثر توغل الجيش السوداني في غرب كردفان وتقدم قوات الدعم السريع في محافظة باو بإقليم النيل الأزرق. وأكدت مصادر إنسانية تحدثت لسودان تربيون أن ردة فعل قوات الدعم السريع على توغل الجيش في عدة مناطق من محلية أبو زبد بولاية غرب كردفان “غرب السودان”، تسببت في انتهاكات شملت القتل والاغتصاب والنهب. وأفادت المصادر ذاتها بأن نحو 2000 نازح جديد من قرى أبو قلب والسعاتة بغرب كردفان، أغلبهم من الأطفال والنساء، وصلوا مدينة الأبيض عاصمة ولاية شمال كردفان في موجة نزوح جديدة وسط ظروف إنسانية بالغة التعقيد، إذ اضطروا للسير لمسافات طويلة. وطبقاً لنازحين جدد تحدثوا لسودان تربيون فإن من بين النازحين الذين تم استيعابهم في المخيمات وأحياء الأبيض، نساءً حوامل ومرضعات، فضلاً عن حدوث حالات وضع وإجهاض خلال رحلة النزوح. وفي إقليم النيل الأزرق أقصى جنوب شرق السودان، قالت مجموعة محامو الطوارئ الحقوقية إن نحو 325 أسرة، “تمثل حوالي 2000 شخص”، نزحت من منطقة مقنزا بمحافظة باو في إقليم النيل الأزرق إلى مدينتي الدمازين والروصيرص، عقب دخول قوات الدعم السريع وحلفائها إلى المنطقة. وحسب المجموعة الحقوقية في بيان اليوم الجمعة، فإن موجة النزوح تثير مخاوف بشأن الأوضاع الإنسانية للأسر النازحة، في ظل احتياجات عاجلة للغذاء ومياه الشرب والإيواء والرعاية الصحية، لا سيما بالنسبة للنساء والأطفال وكبار السن. وحذرت من أن استمرار العمليات العسكرية يهدد بتجدد موجات النزوح من مقنزا والمناطق المجاورة، ويضاعف المخاطر التي يتعرض لها المدنيون. وتشهد منطقة مقنزا نحو 30 كيلومتراً جنوبي مدينة الدمازين عمليات عسكرية وتبادلاً للسيطرة على المنطقة بين الجيش السوداني وتحالف قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية – شمال. ودعت مجموعة محامو الطوارئ قوات الدعم السريع وحلفاءها لضمان حماية المدنيين والامتناع عن ترويع السكان أو تعريض حياتهم وممتلكاتهم للخطر، واستنكرت إطلاق قوات الدعم السريع النار بشكل عشوائي ما تسبب في فرار السكان من المنطقة. كما دعت المنظمات الإنسانية والجهات المعنية إلى إجراء تقييم عاجل لأوضاع النازحين والتدخل لتوفير المساعدات الغذائية والطبية ومياه الشرب ومستلزمات الإيواء، وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية إلى المتضررين. في الأثناء، تمكنت حكومة محافظة الكرمك بإقليم النيل الأزرق بالتعاون مع جهات إنسانية من إجلاء نحو ثلاثين نازحاً أغلبهم من الأطفال والنساء ظلوا عالقين لأكثر من شهر بمنطقة الكيلي جنوب شرق الدمازين عاصمة الإقليم. واستغرقت عملية الإجلاء نحو أسبوعين حتى وصل الفارون إلى مخيم قنيص شرقي الدمازين، على الأقدام لمسافات طويلة. من جانبها قالت مبادرة المجتمع المدني بإقليم النيل الأزرق إن مقاطعة الرنك بولاية أعالي النيل في جنوب السودان استقبلت أكثر من 14 ألف شخص خلال أسبوع واحد فرّوا من تصاعد المواجهات المسلحة في إقليم النيل الأزرق، في موجة نزوح جديدة تعكس اتساع نطاق الأزمة الإنسانية وتزايد المخاطر التي تواجه المدنيين. ووصل النازحون إلى منطقتي شوميدي وقرية أدهم بمقاطعة الرنك، وسط آلاف الأسر إلى مغادرة مناطقها بحثاً عن الأمان، وما يصاحب ذلك من مخاطر الحماية والانتهاكات وفقدان مصادر العيش، فضلاً عن الضغوط المتزايدة على المجتمعات المستضيفة في المناطق الحدودية. الكلمات: السودان، رئيس الوزراء الإثيوبي، معتبرين أنها لا تنفصل عن الخلافات القائمة بين البلدين. الجمعة 2026/11/27 البرهان لا يزال يتمسك بالحسم العسكري الخرطوم - رفضت الحكومة السودانية مبادرة رئيس الوزراء الإثيوبي آبي أحمد لاستضافة حوار شامل بين طرفي الصراع في السودان، معتبرة أنها لا توفر ضمانات حقيقية للتوصل إلى تسوية سياسية، في وقت تتواصل فيه الحرب بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع منذ أكثر من ثلاث سنوات، وسط تعثر المبادرات الإقليمية والدولية الرامية إلى إنهائها. وقال مسؤولان سودانيان، اليوم الجمعة، إن المبادرة الإثيوبية تفتقر إلى الثقة، ولا تنطلق من مقاربة تضمن معالجة جذور الأزمة، في إشارة إلى الخلافات القائمة بين الخرطوم وأديس أبابا بشأن تطورات الصراع السوداني. وكان آبي أحمد قد طرح، الثلاثاء، مبادرة دعا فيها الأطراف السودانية بمختلف مكوناتها العسكرية والسياسية والمدنية إلى المشاركة في حوار شامل تستضيفه بلاده وترعاه، بهدف وقف الحرب والتوصل إلى توافق وطني يؤسس لسلام مستدام. وقال وزير الإعلام بحكومة إقليم دارفور أحمد إسحاق شنب، في تصريح لوكالة الأنباء السودانية، إن المبادرة تثير تساؤلات بشأن توقيتها والظروف المحيطة بها، معتبرا أنها لا تنفصل عن الخلافات القائمة بين البلدين، ومتهما أطرافا داخل إثيوبيا بتقديم دعم لقوات الدعم السريع، وهي اتهامات تنفيها أديس أبابا. وأضاف شنب أن الحكومة السودانية تنظر إلى المبادرة باعتبارها محاولة لمنح الدعم السريع فرصة سياسية في ظل التطورات الميدانية، داعيا إلى معالجة الملفات الأمنية والعسكرية التي تشكل محور الخلاف قبل إطلاق مسارات جديدة للحوار. من جانبه، قال مستشار رئيس الوزراء السوداني مصلح نصار إن المبادرة الإثيوبية لا تحظى بثقة الحكومة، معتبرا أن مواقف أديس أبابا من الأزمة لا توفر أرضية مناسبة للقيام بدور الوسيط. وتعكس هذه التصريحات اتساع فجوة الثقة بين الخرطوم وأديس أبابا، في ظل تبادل الاتهامات بشأن التدخل في الصراع، بعدما أعلنت الحكومة السودانية مطلع نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني الجاري إيداع شكوى لدى مجلس الأمن الدولي ومجلس السلم والأمن الإفريقي، على خلفية اتهامات لإثيوبيا بالضلوع في هجمات استهدفت منشآت مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في عدد من الولايات السودانية وهو ما نفته أديس أبابا. ويأتي رفض المبادرة الإثيوبية في سياق تعثر المساعي السياسية لإنهاء الحرب، إذ سبق أن رفض قائد الجيش السوداني، رئيس مجلس السيادة عبدالفتاح البرهان عدة مبادرات ومقترحات لوقف القتال، ملغما المفاوضات بشروط تتعلق بإنهاء وجود قوات الدعم السريع وانسحابها من المناطق التي تسيطر عليها، وعدم القبول بأي تسوية لا تضمن معالجة الوضع العسكري والأمني. وفي المقابل، أبدت "الدعم السريع" استعدادها للتجاوب مع عدد من المبادرات الإقليمية والدولية الرامية إلى وقف الحرب، وأعلنت في مناسبات عدة قبولها مقترحات لوقف إطلاق النار والانخراط في مسارات تفاوضية، مؤكدة استعدادها للتعامل الإيجابي مع الجهود الرامية إلى إنهاء الصراع. وكان تحالف السودان التأسيسي "تأسيس"، بقيادة قوات الدعم السريع، رحب الثلاثاء بالمبادرة الإثيوبية، وهو ما يعكس استمرار التباين بين طرفي الحرب بشأن الأطراف التي يمكن أن ترعى عملية التفاوض وشروط إطلاقها. وتسعى أطراف إقليمية ودولية إلى دفع الجيش والدعم السريع نحو وقف إطلاق النار وإطلاق عملية سياسية، غير أن الخلافات بشأن ترتيبات المرحلة الانتقالية ومستقبل المؤسسة العسكرية، فضلا عن انعدام الثقة بين الطرفين، لا تزال تعرقل فرص التوصل إلى اتفاق. وتتواصل الحرب في السودان منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، إثر خلافات بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع بشأن توحيد المؤسسة العسكرية، مخلفة عشرات الآلاف من القتلى ونحو 13 مليون نازح، إلى جانب أزمة إنسانية واسعة النطاق تعد من بين الأسوأ 16 منطقة في بلدان منها السودان واليمن وفلسطين والصومال 27 تشرين الثاني/نوفمبر 2026 المساعدات الإنسانية أكدت منظمة الأغذية والزراعة (الفاو) وبرنامج الأغذية العالمي أن ظاهرة النينيو تزيد من حدة العوامل المسببة لانعدام الأمن الغذائي في أكثر مناطق العالم تضررا من الجوع، وحذرتا من أن أجزاء من السودان وجنوب السودان تواجه خطر المجاعة في الأشهر المقبلة. وفي تقريرهما المشترك الأخير، الذي يغطي الفترة من كانون الأول/ديسمبر المقبل وحتى مايو/أيار 2027، حددت الوكالتان الأمميتان 16 دولة باعتبارها "بؤرا ساخنة للجوع"، ويعد السودان وجنوب السودان والصومال وأجزاء من نيجيريا واليمن الأكثر إثارة للقلق من بينها. وفي تصريحات للصحفيين في جنيف عبر الفيديو من روما، أوضح رين بولسن مدير مكتب الطوارئ والصمود لدى الفاو ، أن النزاعات والعنف لا تزال تمثل السبب الرئيسي للجوع في معظم هذه الدول، إلى جانب الضغوط الاقتصادية والاضطرابات التي تؤثر على التجارة العالمية وسلاسل التوريد. وأشار إلى أن "التحديات المحيطة بمضيق هرمز والبحر الأسود والبحر الأحمر تؤثر على تكاليف المدخلات الزراعية والسلع الأساسية الأخرى، وتلحق الضرر بشكل خاص بالأسر الأكثر ضعفا والتي تعاني من انعدام الأمن الغذائي". عامل جوهري، ولكن.. وأضاف بولسن أن ظاهرة الـنينيو تعد أيضا عاملا جوهريا في التوقعات الواردة في التقرير، حيث بدأت بالفعل في إحداث تداعيات عالمية تؤثر على العديد من بؤر الجوع. لكنه شدد على أنه لا يمكن النظر إلى هذه الظاهرة "بمعزل عن غيرها، فهي في الواقع عامل إضافي يفاقم تداعيات النزاعات والعنف والضغوط الأخرى". وقال إن تأثيرات النينيو تختلف من منطقة إلى أخرى. ففي جنوبي أفريقيا، تؤثر موجات الجفاف وارتفاع درجات الحرارة على الموسم الزراعي، بينما تواجه شرق أفريقيا، ولا سيما منطقة القرن الأفريقي، خطر حدوث فيضانات شديدة قد تؤدي إلى "تدمير المحاصيل، وتشريد الأسر، وتعطيل الأسواق، فضلا عن عرقلة قدرتنا على تقديم المساعدات الإنسانية". ERR-Taweela تعتمد آلاف الأسر السودانية على مبادرات شبابية محلية تقدم الإغاثة، وتنظم ملاجئ ومطابخ مجتمعية لمواجهة الجوع والمرض. توقعات يمكن تجنبها وأكد بولسن أنه يمكن تجنب هذه السيناريوهات المتوقعة "إذا قدمت المساعدات في الوقت المناسب، بما يضمن الوصول إلى الغذاء، وحماية المحاصيل والثروة الحيوانية، والحفاظ على سبل العيش". وأوضح أن تحذير الوكالتين الأمميتين يهدف إلى "دعم الأسر قبل أن تضطر إلى استنفاد كل ما تبقى لديها من موارد أو اللجوء إلى استراتيجيات التكيف الطارئة من أجل البقاء". وقال: "نعلم أين تكمن المخاطر، ولدينا أدلة تدعم ذلك، لذا يتعين علينا التحرك قبل أن تتحول هذه المخاطر إلى كوارث". استمرار الضغوط على سلاسل التوريد وانضم إلى بولسن، جان مارتن باور مدير تحليل الأمن الغذائي لدى برنامج الأغذية العالمي ، والذي سلط الضوء على "نقاط الاختناق الثلاث" التي تؤثر على الاقتصاد العالمي، معتبرا إياها عاملا رئيسيا في تفاقم الجوع في البلدان المذكورة في التقرير. وأشار إلى أن الأحداث في مضيق هرمز والبحر الأسود والبحر الأحمر كانت لها تداعيات وخيمة على عمليات الشحن، وتكاليف التأمين، وأسعار الوقود، وأسواق الطاقة، والأسمدة، "وفي نهاية المطاف على أسعار الغذاء"، مما زاد من صعوبة حياة ملايين الأسر حول العالم. وشدد على أنه في حال استمرت الضغوط على سلاسل التوريد العالمية حتى منتصف العام المقبل، فسيواجه البرنامج تكاليف إضافية تصل إلى 750 مليون دولار، مما سيجعله عاجزا عن تقديم المساعدة لأكثر من سبعة ملايين شخص من أصل 91 مليونا يهدف البرنامج للوصول إليهم. كما أشار باور إلى أن الموارد المخصصة لمعالجة قضايا الغذاء والتغذية في بؤر الجوع الخمس الأكثر إثارة للقلق قد انخفضت بنسبة 62% منذ عام 2022. وأكد أن توفير التمويل الكامل قد يمنح مزيدا من الوقت، لكن المطلوب أيضا هو ضمان الوصول الآمن، بالإضافة إلى "دعم دبلوماسي لإنهاء النزاعات التي تقف وراء جزء كبير من حالات الجوع التي نسلط الضوء عليها في هذا التقرير". تجدر الإشارة إلى أن التقرير صنف أربع دول على أنها تثير قلقا بالغا، وهي أفغانستان، وجمهورية الكونغو الديمقراطية، وهايتي، وفلسطين. وذكر التقرير أنه على الرغم من بدء تحسن الأمن الغذائي في قطاع غزة عقب وقف إطلاق النار في تشرين الأول/أكتوبر 2025، إلا أن هذه المكاسب تظل هشة، ومن المتوقع أن يتفاقم انعدام الأمن الغذائي الحاد في الضفة الغربية. ♦ تحميل تطبيق أخبار الأمم المتحدة بالعربية من متجر آبل لأجهزة الأيفون والآيباد IOS أو من متجر غوغل لأجهزة أندرويد Android . ♦ يعلن استعادة السيطرة على "مقنزا" بالنيل الأزرق ومبادرة مدنية أفادت بنزوح أكثر من 14 ألف شخص إلى جنوب السودان خلال أسبوع Adel Abdelrheem 27 نوفمبر 2026 • تحديث : 27 نوفمبر 2026 photo : صفحة القوات المسلحة السودانية / AA SUDAN عادل عبد الرحيم / الأناضول أعلن الجيش السوداني، الجمعة، استعادة السيطرة على منطقة "مقنزا" بولاية النيل الأزرق جنوب شرقي البلاد، بعد معارك مع قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية/ شمال. وقالت الفرقة الرابعة مشاة التابعة للجيش، في بيان، إن قواتها استعادت السيطرة على المنطقة وطردت منها عناصر الدعم السريع، فيما لم يصدر تعليق فوري من الأخيرة. وتقع منطقة "مقنزا" جنوبي مدينة الدمازين، عاصمة ولاية النيل الأزرق. ** موجة نزوح جديدة وفي السياق، قالت مبادرة المجتمع المدني بولاية النيل الأزرق (مستقلة)، الجمعة، إن مقاطعة الرنك بولاية أعالي النيل في جنوب السودان استقبلت أكثر من 14 ألف شخص خلال أسبوع، فروا من المواجهات المتصاعدة في النيل الأزرق. وأوضحت أن معظم الوافدين وصلوا إلى منطقتي "شوميدي" و"قرية أدهم"، وسط احتياجات متزايدة إلى الغذاء والمياه الصالحة للشرب والمأوى والرعاية الصحية. وأعربت المبادرة عن قلقها إزاء فقدان الأسر مصادر رزقها وتزايد الضغوط على المجتمعات المضيفة. ودعت إلى الوقف الفوري للأعمال العدائية وحماية المدنيين وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية دون عوائق. والثلاثاء الماضي، اتهمت السلطات السودانية قوات الدعم السريع باستهداف مدينتي الدمازين والروصيرص بطائرة مسيّرة، ما أسفر عن مقتل 17 شخصا وإصابة العشرات، دون تعليق من الدعم السريع. ** تصعيد عسكري والأربعاء، أعلن الجيش السوداني وصول قوات "درع السودان" إلى ولاية النيل الأزرق لإسناد قواته. وفي اليوم نفسه، أفادت مصادر عسكرية للأناضول بأن الجيش، بمساندة قوات حليفة، استعاد منطقة "سودا" بالولاية، بعد يومين من إعلان الدعم السريع السيطرة عليها. وتشهد ولاية النيل الأزرق تصعيدا عسكريا منذ أيام، على خلفية هجمات شنتها قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية/ شمال المتحالفة معها على مناطق عدة بالولاية. وتتفاقم المعاناة الإنسانية في السودان جراء الحرب بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع، المستمرة منذ أبريل/ نيسان 2023 إثر خلاف بشأن توحيد المؤسسة العسكرية، والتي أسفرت عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص. The commitment was reiterated today by State Minister of Foreign Affairs Ambassador Hadera Abera during talks with Anita Kiki Gbeho, Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General for South Sudan and Head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS). According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the two sides exchanged views on South Sudan’s upcoming elections, the prevailing political and security situation, and the implementation of the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS). They also discussed the operational challenges facing UNMISS and the activities of the AU–IGAD–UN Task Force. During the meeting, Ambassador Hadera reiterated Ethiopia’s full support for UNMISS and its mandate. He further emphasized the country’s commitment to working closely with South Sudanese stakeholders, as well as regional and international partners, to advance sustainable peace and security in the nation. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

In a statement dated Nov. 26, the research and documentation division of Eritrea's foreign ministry said Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party was trying to "manufacture a veneer of international legitimacy" around its demand for "sovereign sea access". It cited a workshop in late October on maritime security and search-and-rescue operations, led by the Ethiopian navy and supported by the European Union. The workshop brought together naval representatives from Somalia's Puntland and Somaliland regions and from Djibouti, while "pointedly bypassing the Federal Government of Somalia in favour of regional administrations", the statement said. "A genuinely technical workshop on navigational safety does not begin by undermining the recognized sovereignty of a coastal state," it said. The statement also said Ethiopian army chief Field Marshal Birhanu Jula told representatives in the Tigray regional capital Mekele on Nov. 13 that Dogali, Gundet and Adulis, areas in Eritrea, belonged to Tigray. It said he also claimed that the port of Zeila, in northwestern Somalia, was originally Ethiopian. "Non-littoral actors possess neither the geographical standing nor the sovereign mandate to dictate the security architecture governing the Red Sea," the Eritrean statement said. It cited a joint declaration signed by the leaders of Eritrea, Egypt, Somalia and Sudan in El Alamein on Oct. 4, which said governance of the Red Sea was the exclusive prerogative of coastal states. Eritrea said it had never opposed commercial use of its ports by Ethiopia, provided its sovereignty was respected, and that it would "not surrender an inch of its territory or maritime domain". The statement urged European and multilateral donors funding maritime initiatives that involve landlocked states with "publicly declared expansionist agenda" to reflect on the consequences of their support. There was no immediate comment from Ethiopia's government. In a statement issued Thursday, Eritrea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Prosperity Party government of seeking to "manufacture a veneer of international legitimacy" around its demand for "sovereign sea access," which Asmara characterized as territorial revisionism. The statement follows Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's address to the House of Peoples' Representatives on Thursday, November 26, in which he rejected claims that Ethiopia intends to invade Eritrea , but reiterated that access to the Red Sea remains a strategic imperative to be pursued through dialogue. Invasion is not needed; we want it peacefully and through dialogue," Abiy told lawmakers, likening Ethiopia's maritime ambitions to the natural course of the Abay River. Abiy claimed Ethiopia had made repeated efforts to pursue economic cooperation with Eritrea, including proposals to extend electricity infrastructure, build roads and jointly develop a port, but said the Eritrean government had rejected them. "We have made high efforts with the Eritrean government to develop together," he said, citing a proposal to supply electricity at Ethiopian domestic prices and jointly undertake infrastructure projects. He also said Ethiopia had undergone a "strategic awakening" after its political elite failed to properly recognize the country's Red Sea interests, arguing that neighboring countries should recognize the long-term strategic implications of the issue. Abiy further warned that Ethiopia's size and population meant instability within the country would have far-reaching regional consequences, cautioning against scenarios involving millions of Ethiopians moving into neighboring states. "Because we are a large population; our disturbance disturbs many," he said, arguing that Ethiopia's stability was central to wider regional peace. He also pointed to shifting geopolitical dynamics, including the potential opening of Arctic shipping routes, arguing that these could alter the Red Sea's strategic importance in the coming years. Eritrea, however, said Ethiopia's maritime diplomacy was increasingly being used to normalize the involvement of a landlocked country in Red Sea security arrangements. It cited a late-October maritime security and search-and-rescue workshop in Addis Abeba , supported by the European Union. The workshop brought together naval representatives from Puntland and Somaliland alongside representatives from Djibouti. Asmara argued that including Somali regional administrations while bypassing the Federal Government of Somalia undermined the sovereignty of a recognized coastal state. Eritrea also cited the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, held in Bahir Dar from October 23-25, where National Intelligence and Security Service Director General Redwan Hussein argued that Ethiopia should have a role in Red Sea security arrangements given the waterway's strategic importance and growing involvement of global powers. Redwan maintained that Red Sea security was not a responsibility reserved exclusively for coastal states, a position Eritrea said reflected Addis Abeba's efforts to expand its role in regional maritime affairs. The Eritrean statement further cited Field Marshal Birhanu Jula's November 13 remarks in Mekele, in which he reportedly asserted that Dogali, Gundet and Adulis belonged to Tigray and made claims concerning Somalia's port of Zeila. Asmara described the remarks as part of a broader territorial narrative advanced by Ethiopian political and military officials. It warned that repeated territorial assertions by senior officials, alongside threats to secure maritime access through force, challenged regional sovereignty and internationally recognized borders. The statement invoked Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of states. ethiopia.title: Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia of Using Maritime Diplomacy to 'Camouflage Its Irredentist Ambitions'
ethiopia.content: Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia of Using Maritime Diplomacy to 'Camouflage Its Irredentist Ambitions' - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia of Using Maritime Diplomacy to 'Camouflage Its Irredentist Ambitions' Pixabay, Pixabay Drapeau de l'Ethiopie et de l'Erythrée 27 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Eritrea has accused Ethiopia of using maritime diplomacy and regional security forums to mask what it described as territorial ambitions in the Horn of Africa, escalating tensions amid renewed disagreements over Ethiopia's pursuit of Red Sea access. In a statement issued Thursday, Eritrea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Prosperity Party government of seeking to "manufacture a veneer of international legitimacy" around its demand for "sovereign sea access," which Asmara characterized as territorial revisionism. The statement follows Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's address to the House of Peoples' Representatives on Thursday, November 26, in which he rejected claims that Ethiopia intends to invade Eritrea , but reiterated that access to the Red Sea remains a strategic imperative to be pursued through dialogue. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Now they say, 'Ethiopia is going to invade Eritrea, Ethiopia will wage an invasion for the Red Sea'--we will not wage an invasion. Invasion is not needed; we want it peacefully and through dialogue," Abiy told lawmakers, likening Ethiopia's maritime ambitions to the natural course of the Abay River. Abiy claimed Ethiopia had made repeated efforts to pursue economic cooperation with Eritrea, including proposals to extend electricity infrastructure, build roads and jointly develop a port, but said the Eritrean government had rejected them. "We have made high efforts with the Eritrean government to develop together," he said, citing a proposal to supply electricity at Ethiopian domestic prices and jointly undertake infrastructure projects. He also said Ethiopia had undergone a "strategic awakening" after its political elite failed to properly recognize the country's Red Sea interests, arguing that neighboring countries should recognize the long-term strategic implications of the issue. Abiy further warned that Ethiopia's size and population meant instability within the country would have far-reaching regional consequences, cautioning against scenarios involving millions of Ethiopians moving into neighboring states. "Because we are a large population; our disturbance disturbs many," he said, arguing that Ethiopia's stability was central to wider regional peace. He also pointed to shifting geopolitical dynamics, including the potential opening of Arctic shipping routes, arguing that these could alter the Red Sea's strategic importance in the coming years. Eritrea, however, said Ethiopia's maritime diplomacy was increasingly being used to normalize the involvement of a landlocked country in Red Sea security arrangements. It cited a late-October maritime security and search-and-rescue workshop in Addis Abeba , supported by the European Union. The workshop brought together naval representatives from Puntland and Somaliland alongside representatives from Djibouti. Asmara argued that including Somali regional administrations while bypassing the Federal Government of Somalia undermined the sovereignty of a recognized coastal state. Eritrea also cited the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, held in Bahir Dar from October 23-25, where National Intelligence and Security Service Director General Redwan Hussein argued that Ethiopia should have a role in Red Sea security arrangements given the waterway's strategic importance and growing involvement of global powers. Redwan maintained that Red Sea security was not a responsibility reserved exclusively for coastal states, a position Eritrea said reflected Addis Abeba's efforts to expand its role in regional maritime affairs. The Eritrean statement further cited Field Marshal Birhanu Jula's November 13 remarks in Mekele, in which he reportedly asserted that Dogali, Gundet and Adulis belonged to Tigray and made claims concerning Somalia's port of Zeila. Asmara described the remarks as part of a broader territorial narrative advanced by Ethiopian political and military officials. It warned that repeated territorial assertions by senior officials, alongside threats to secure maritime access through force, challenged regional sovereignty and internationally recognized borders. The statement invoked Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of states. Eritrea claimed it had previously offered Ethiopia access to the ports of Assab and Massawa, including proposals in 2000 and 2002 to facilitate humanitarian assistance, which it said Addis Abeba rejected. ethiopia.title: COP32 Offers Ethiopia a Strategic Path to Green Growth and Global Influence
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: COP32 Offers Ethiopia a Strategic Path to Green Growth and Global Influence - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: COP32 Offers Ethiopia a Strategic Path to Green Growth and Global Influence 27 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) When world leaders, policymakers, climate negotiators, investors, and development partners gather in Addis Ababa from November 8 to 19, 2027, for the 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32), Ethiopia will take center stage in global climate diplomacy at a defining moment for the country and the African continent. Hosting the summit presents Ethiopia with a historic opportunity to strengthen its international standing, mobilize climate finance, attract green investment, deepen development partnerships, and accelerate its transition toward a climate-resilient, low-carbon economy. Beyond convening one of the world's largest diplomatic gatherings, COP32 provides Ethiopia with a powerful platform to place Africa's climate priorities at the heart of global negotiations while showcasing its progress in renewable energy, environmental restoration, sustainable transport, and green development. The opportunity also carries significant political and economic weight. For Ethiopia, COP32 is not simply an international conference to be organized and successfully delivered. It is an opportunity to translate diplomatic leadership into concrete development gains, positioning the country as a destination for climate investment and a prominent voice in shaping the future of global climate cooperation. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Ethiopia secured the hosting role following unanimous endorsement by the African Group of Negotiators at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025, after Nigeria withdrew its competing bid in support of a unified African candidacy. The endorsement reflected continental confidence in Ethiopia's diplomatic standing and its growing engagement in international climate affairs. The conference also builds on Ethiopia's experience hosting the Second Africa Climate Summit in September 2025, which attracted more than 25,000 participants and produced the Addis Ababa Declaration. As the headquarters of the African Union, Addis Ababa is uniquely positioned to bring together world leaders, policymakers, development partners, climate experts, and investors. The Strategic Value of COP32 The strategic value of COP32 extends far beyond international recognition. It offers Ethiopia an opportunity to mobilize financing for renewable energy, climate-smart agriculture, resilient infrastructure, forest restoration, clean technologies, and sustainable urban development. It also provides a critical platform for advocating accessible, predictable, affordable, and concessional climate finance for African countries, which have contributed relatively little to historical global emissions but face disproportionately severe climate impacts. At COP29 in Baku, countries agreed on a new climate finance goal calling on developed countries to take the lead in mobilizing at least 300 billion USD annually for developing nations by 2035, within a broader ambition to scale climate finance from all sources to 1.3 trillion USD annually. Ethiopia can use its COP32 presidency to advocate for practical mechanisms that translate these commitments into accessible financing for vulnerable economies. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has consistently emphasized that climate action must be viewed as an economic and development priority rather than a narrowly environmental concern. Addressing the opening of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026, he stated: "In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy." The statement captures an important dimension of Ethiopia's approach to climate change: environmental protection, economic transformation, agricultural productivity, energy development, and livelihood security are interconnected priorities. During the same conference, the Prime Minister called for climate financing that reaches vulnerable communities before disasters occur, stressing: "Funding should be agreed in advance. It can then move at the speed of our forecasters, while there is still time to save lives." These remarks offer a clear indication of the priorities Ethiopia intends to advance as it prepares to assume a prominent role in international climate diplomacy through COP32. Prime Minister Abiy has also highlighted the broader national benefits of hosting the conference. In convening the COP32 National Steering Committee on November 16, 2026, he described the summit as an opportunity to advance Ethiopia's climate and environmental agenda, strengthen international partnerships, attract investment, and translate national initiatives into lasting development outcomes. He further emphasized the need for a coordinated, whole-of-government approach to ensure that preparations are aligned and the country is ready to deliver a successful international conference. Domestic Transformation: Building Credibility Through Action Ethiopia's ambition to host COP32 is anchored in domestic initiatives demonstrating its commitment to environmental protection, renewable energy, and climate-resilient development. One of the most visible is the Green Legacy Initiative, launched in 2019. The nationwide program has mobilized millions of citizens in large-scale tree-planting and environmental restoration campaigns. Government figures indicate that more than 56 billion seedlings have been planted through the initiative, reflecting the scale of the country's efforts to restore degraded landscapes and expand green spaces. The initiative has become an important component of Ethiopia's environmental diplomacy. It also demonstrates how public participation can support national environmental objectives while creating awareness about the importance of protecting natural resources. Speaking at the Second Africa Climate Summit in Addis Ababa in September 2025, Prime Minister Abiy highlighted the initiative as an example of Ethiopia's homegrown climate solutions. He also articulated a broader African ambition, declaring: "We are not here to negotiate our survival. We are here to design the world's next climate economy." The statement reflects Ethiopia's intention to move beyond the conventional portrayal of Africa as merely a victim of climate change and instead position the continent as an active contributor to global climate solutions. In the energy sector, Ethiopia has steadily expanded its renewable electricity generation capacity through investments in hydropower, wind, and solar energy. The inauguration of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) in September 2025 marked a major milestone in the country's ambition to strengthen clean energy generation, expand electricity access, and increase regional power exports. Ethiopia has also taken significant steps toward sustainable transport. Since January 2024, the country has restricted imports of conventional petrol- and diesel-powered vehicles as part of its transition toward electric mobility. Although expanding charging infrastructure, ensuring vehicle affordability, and strengthening electricity distribution remain important priorities, the policy positions Ethiopia as an early mover in Africa's clean transport transition. These initiatives complement Ethiopia's updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), which targets a reduction in projected greenhouse gas emissions of up to 70.3 percent below business-as-usual levels by 2035, contingent on international support, alongside a long-term ambition of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. However, Ethiopia's climate agenda extends beyond emissions reduction. Climate change poses significant risks to agriculture, food security, water resources, and rural livelihoods. World Bank assessments have estimated that climate impacts could cost the country between 1 and 1.5 percent of GDP annually, with the potential for substantially greater losses in the coming decades. Consequently, adaptation financing, climate-resilient agriculture, water resource management, early-warning systems, and disaster preparedness must remain central priorities in Ethiopia's preparations for COP32. This is particularly important given the Prime Minister's recent emphasis on early action and financial support for vulnerable communities. At COP31, he underscored the urgency of ensuring that climate finance is available when early warnings are issued and reaches those most exposed to climate risks. His appeal was particularly powerful when he observed: "Our farmers once trusted the seasons to arrive on time. Let us make sure our support does." The statement captures the human dimension of climate change and reinforces the importance of ensuring that international climate commitments produce tangible benefits for communities whose livelihoods depend on increasingly unpredictable weather patterns. Advancing Africa's Climate Priorities COP32 will give Ethiopia an influential platform to amplify Africa's collective position in international climate negotiations, particularly on climate finance, technology transfer, adaptation, and loss and damage. For African countries, the central challenge is balancing the urgent need for industrialization, energy access, employment creation, and agricultural modernization with the growing threats posed by climate change. Ethiopia can use its COP32 presidency to champion a development framework that recognizes Africa's right to economic transformation while supporting clean energy, environmental protection, and climate resilience. At the Second Africa Climate Summit, Prime Minister Abiy offered a particularly important perspective on the continent's position in the global climate economy. He called for a shift in how international partners approach Africa's climate ambitions, stating: "It is time to replace climate aid with climate investment. This is not charity. It is the most strategic investment humanity can make." This position could become a defining theme of Ethiopia's COP32 diplomacy. Rather than treating Africa primarily as a recipient of climate assistance, Ethiopia can advocate for investment partnerships that recognize the continent's enormous renewable energy potential, agricultural resources, biodiversity, critical minerals, and young population. The continent has considerable opportunities to develop solar, wind, geothermal, and hydropower resources, expand green industrialization, strengthen sustainable agriculture, and build climate-resilient infrastructure. However, realizing these opportunities requires affordable financing, technology transfer, capacity building, and stronger international partnerships. COP32 should therefore provide a platform for moving beyond declarations toward practical investment agreements, bankable projects, and measurable implementation commitments. The summit will also offer Ethiopia an opportunity to showcase its tourism potential, biodiversity, cultural heritage, and emerging economic opportunities. From the historical landmarks of Aksum and Lalibela to the Simien and Bale Mountains, the Great Rift Valley, and Lake Tana, Ethiopia possesses considerable natural and cultural assets that can reinforce its broader green growth narrative. Hosting thousands of international delegates will also generate economic opportunities across tourism, hospitality, transport, construction, and other service industries. Investments in conference facilities, urban infrastructure, transport networks, accommodation, and digital connectivity could produce economic benefits extending well beyond the summit. Turning COP32 into Lasting National Gains With less than a year remaining before the summit opens, effective implementation will be decisive in turning Ethiopia's hosting responsibilities into lasting national benefits. The government's establishment of coordination structures and engagement with international partners, alongside Prime Minister Abiy's convening of the National Steering Committee, signals the importance attached to a coordinated national preparation process. Successful delivery will require targeted investments in conference venues, hospitality, public transport, security, telecommunications, and urban environmental management. Equally important will be the participation of the private sector, universities, research institutions, civil society organizations, youth groups, and local communities. The private sector, in particular, has an important role to play in converting the international attention generated by COP32 into investment opportunities. Businesses operating in renewable energy, electric mobility, construction, agriculture, tourism, manufacturing, and financial services should be encouraged to develop partnerships and investment proposals ahead of the conference. Ethiopia must also ensure that its domestic climate achievements are supported by transparent implementation and measurable results. Expanding last-mile electricity access, scaling up clean cooking solutions, strengthening electric vehicle infrastructure, improving climate-smart agricultural practices, and monitoring the long-term survival of planted trees are among the important benchmarks that can demonstrate progress. The conference should also provide an opportunity to strengthen Ethiopia's institutional capacity for climate finance mobilization, project preparation, environmental governance, and international partnership management. Ultimately, the country's credibility as a climate host will depend not only on its ability to organize a successful international gathering but also on its capacity to demonstrate that its climate ambitions are translating into practical development outcomes. A Defining Opportunity for Ethiopia and Africa COP32 represents both an international responsibility and a defining national opportunity for Ethiopia. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's vision of moving from climate aid toward climate investment, combined with his emphasis on early action, accessible financing, and climate-resilient development, provides an important foundation for shaping Ethiopia's engagement with the international community. The country's presidency can help advance a more balanced global climate agenda--one that recognizes Africa's development aspirations, acknowledges its disproportionate vulnerability to climate impacts, and creates opportunities for the continent to participate more meaningfully in the emerging global green economy. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to ensure that the diplomatic visibility and international partnerships generated by COP32 translate into renewable energy investments, stronger infrastructure, employment opportunities, improved livelihoods, and greater climate resilience. The ultimate measure of Ethiopia's COP32 presidency will not simply be the successful organization of a global summit in Addis Ababa. It will be the extent to which the conference helps convert international commitments into tangible investments, strengthens Africa's voice in global climate governance, and delivers lasting benefits for Ethiopians and the wider African continent. Amos Lugoloobi, held bilateral consultations yesterday, 25 November 2026, with Ambassador Lencho Bati, Director-General of the Ethiopian Diaspora Service (EDS). The engagement forms a central pillar of Uganda's five-day benchmarking mission to the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia (23-27 November 2026), aimed at adapting proven legal, institutional, financial, and digital mechanisms to operationalise Uganda's first comprehensive National Diaspora Support and Engagement Policy. Uganda's Vision: Moving Beyond Remittances to Investment and Technology Transfer Addressing the meeting, Hon. Amos Lugoloobi noted that His Excellency President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni specifically tasked the delegation with visiting Addis Ababa to study Ethiopia's transformation and pioneering diaspora engagement frameworks. Hon. Lugoloobi highlighted the shared history between the two nations and acknowledged the vital role remittances play in stabilizing Uganda's currency and supporting debt servicing, with inflows having more than doubled from approximately USD 1.4 billion in 2024 to USD 3.03 billion in FY 2025/26. "Uganda has a large diaspora, particularly in the United Kingdom, whose remittances already play a crucial role in supporting our economy," said Hon. Amos Lugoloobi. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "However, we now wish to move beyond just remittances. We are here to learn from Ethiopia's remarkable success in leveraging its diaspora for flagship national projects like the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, and to adopt institutional arrangements for mapping diaspora skills, driving technology transfer, and expanding productive investment." The Ugandan delegation, comprising senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED), Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), Office of the Solicitor General, State House, Bank of Uganda (BoU), Capital Markets Authority (CMA), National Planning Authority (NPA), and Ministry of Internal Affairs, sought detailed insights into diaspora registration systems, investor safeguards, and capital-market instruments. Ethiopia's Experience: National Cohesion, Flagship Projects, and Origin Identification Welcoming the Ugandan delegation, Ambassador Lencho Bati underscored the importance of shifting the global narrative around African immigrants from negative stereotypes to recognizing their massive contributions as cultural, financial, and tourism ambassadors. Ambassador Bati shared how integrating the diaspora into national reconciliation efforts and Vision 2050 has fostered healing, unity, and substantial capital inflows. Somalia's third-generation passport was unveiled at a meeting of East Africa's meeting immigration chiefs. / Others Somalia has presented its new third-generation electronic passport to East African Community (EAC) member states, marking another step towards regional integration and the modernisation of its immigration system. The passport was showcased during a three-day meeting of immigration chiefs in Kampala, Uganda, which concluded on Thursday. Somalia’s delegation was led by Hussein Qasim Yusuf, Director-General of the Immigration and Citizenship Agency, who briefed regional officials on the passport’s advanced security features and technology. advertisements The new travel document incorporates modern security measures while reflecting Somalia’s national identity, cultural heritage and traditions. The meeting focused on implementing EAC Council of Ministers’ decisions, harmonising immigration procedures and improving cooperation between member states. Officials also discussed the recognition of national identity cards, the modernisation of immigration services and measures to facilitate the movement of people across the region. EAC passport integration The presentation follows Somalia’s approval to adopt and issue the EAC electronic passport, a key requirement in the country’s efforts to align its travel documents with regional standards. In February 2026, Somalia’s Ambassador to Tanzania and Permanent Representative to the EAC, Ilyas Ali Hassan, formally handed over the authorisation to Somali Internal Security Minister Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail, known as Fartaag. The authorisation, granted in December 2025, allowed Somalia to adopt the EAC passport’s approved design and proceed with preparations for its issuance. Somalia has since been working to modernise its travel documentation and strengthen immigration cooperation with other member states. The EAC electronic passport was first launched during the bloc’s 17th Ordinary Heads of State Summit on 2 March 2016. It is issued in three categories: ordinary, service and diplomatic passports, replacing older national passports in participating countries. The document is designed to strengthen travel security, improve border management and facilitate regional mobility. Somalia officially joined the East African Community on 4 March 2024, becoming the regional bloc’s eighth member state. Since joining, Mogadishu has been working to align its policies and institutions with regional commitments, particularly in immigration, trade and the movement of people. The introduction of the electronic passport represents another step towards meeting those obligations and strengthening Somalia’s participation in the regional bloc. According to the latest Henley Passport Index, Somalia ranks 99th globally, with its passport providing access to 32 destinations without a prior visa. In a statement issued Thursday, Nov. 26, the Uganda Peoples' Defence Forces (UPDF) said Aviation Unit VI was officially flagged off during a ceremony at Soroti Air Force Base in eastern Uganda. advertisements The unit will be commanded by Col. Simon Andiandu, with Maj. Ssempa Ndaula serving as deputy commander. The ceremony was presided over by Ugandan Air Force Commander Lt. Gen. Charles Okidi, who urged the deploying personnel to maintain discipline, professionalism and teamwork while carrying out their mission in Somalia. “This ceremony here today marks the formal deployment of Aviation Unit VI under UGABAG XLVIII. This is a testament to our continued effort and unwavering commitment to regional peace, security and stability on the African continent,” Okidi said. He told the troops that their deployment carried significant responsibilities and urged them to remain committed despite the challenges they could encounter during their mission. The Chief of Staff of the Ugandan Air Force, Brig. Gen. James Itungo, also addressed the personnel, describing them as representatives of Uganda and urging them to demonstrate professionalism and sound judgment throughout their deployment. Itungo called on the troops to remain alert to the operational environment and carry out their duties with confidence and discipline. Soroti Air Force Wing Commander Brig. Gen. Collin Mbaga Nkwasibwe said the personnel had undergone specialized training tailored to their operational responsibilities, including engineering and aviation security. The UPDF statement did not disclose the number of personnel being deployed, the aircraft assigned to the unit or the specific locations where they would operate in Somalia. The deployment comes just days after Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni met in Entebbe on Nov. 23 and called for intensified military operations against al-Shabab. In a joint communiqué, the two leaders emphasized the need for predictable and sustainable funding for AUSSOM and alternative financing arrangements to support forces deployed under bilateral security agreements. Uganda has played a major role in African Union military operations in Somalia since 2007, contributing ground troops and other military capabilities to successive peacekeeping missions. However, Kampala has recently begun withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral arrangements with Somalia and has outlined plans for a gradual drawdown of its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027. The deployment of Aviation Unit VI comes amid those broader discussions about the future of Uganda's military presence and the transfer of security responsibilities to Somali forces. The UPDF did not indicate whether the aviation unit would replace an existing contingent or increase the number of Ugandan personnel serving under AUSSOM. AUSSOM, which succeeded the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) in January 2025, supports Somali security forces in operations against al-Shabab and the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to national institutions. Uganda remains one of the mission's key troop-contributing countries as Somali and African Union officials seek continued international support for counterterrorism operations and the security transition. The president said Somalia’s partnership with Türkiye had delivered tangible results despite criticism and what he described as misinformation surrounding the bilateral defence and economic cooperation agreement. The ceremony marked the start of construction of a new naval headquarters, a Maritime Operations Coordination Centre and facilities for handling naval vessels at the Turkish Naval Task Force’s Barbaros Camp. The projects are intended to strengthen Somalia’s maritime defence capabilities and support the rebuilding of its naval forces. Somalia’s maritime security vital to global trade Mohamud stressed that protecting Somalia’s coastline and maritime resources was essential not only to national security but also to stability across the Horn of Africa. “Our security depends on protecting our waters. The security of Africa and the Horn of Africa depends on protecting our waters,” he said. “Global security, trade and economic activity also depend on our waters being safe.” The president said Somalia’s vast maritime territory required a capable, well-equipped navy to protect its resources and maintain security along key international shipping routes. He highlighted the country’s strategic location along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden, where commercial vessels travel between Asia, Africa and Europe. REUTERS/Feisal Omar/File Photo Hunger is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, with famine threatening parts of Africa, two United Nations agencies warned on Friday. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) said Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen faced the gravest threats, driven by conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather. The number of hunger hotspots has risen from 13 in the previous report released in June, with Chad, Uganda, and parts of both southern Africa and Central America added to the list, while Lebanon was removed. In the latest joint report covering December 2026 to May 2027, the agencies warned ⁠that shrinking humanitarian ⁠funding was undermining efforts to avert catastrophe. Aid for the five countries facing the gravest hunger threats fell by two-thirds between 2022 and 2025, said Conor Elliott, a senior official in FAO's emergencies and resilience office. "These are huge changes in international support," he said, warning that the cuts were also undermining the collection of data needed to assess ⁠the scale of the crisis. According to Reuters, the report said armed conflict and violence were driving hunger in 12 of the 16 hotspots, while soaring food, energy and transport costs were further eroding people's ability to feed themselves. The agencies said the developing El Niño weather pattern could aggravate the crisis, bringing drought and extreme temperatures to southern Africa and parts of central America, and potentially destructive flooding to parts of eastern Africa. "There's going to be a very, very strong El Niño effect," said Elliott, warning that some areas were likely to ⁠swing from drought ⁠conditions to heavy rains in the coming months. In Sudan, famine is a risk in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan through January 2027, with fighting disrupting food production, markets and aid deliveries. The agencies also identified famine risks among displaced people in Somalia's Baidoa region and in parts of South Sudan, where escalating violence has compounded an already desperate humanitarian situation. Afghanistan, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Palestinian enclave Gaza were also classified as areas of very high concern. Gaza was downgraded from the highest level of concern following improvements in food security since an October 2025 ceasefire, although the agencies warned that conditions remained severe and fragile. Lisbon Police Department Investigating Shots Fired Incident Facebook Twitter Instagram YouTube Friday, November 27 Home Topics Business Commentary Crime Education Energy & Environment Healthcare Housing Immigration Maine and New England News Politics Maine Wire TV Blog About Us Contact Us Support Us Store Home » News » News » America’s Long-Running War On Terror Mission In Somalia Gets Another Chapter News · Published November 27, 2026 at 10:40 am America’s Long-Running War On Terror Mission In Somalia Gets Another Chapter By Jillian Butler, DCNF Reporter, Daily Caller News Foundation DCNF 3 Comments 3 4 Mins Read 4 Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email By Jillian Butler, DCNF Reporter, Daily Caller News Foundation American military officials have reportedly returned to a Somali airbase just weeks after withdrawing, extending Washington’s decades-long counterterrorism mission in the African nation. U.S. personnel are expected to resume operations at Baledogle Airbase following reports that American security contractor Bancroft Global Development secured a new agreement to train Somali special forces battling al-Shabab, as per independent Somali outlet Kaab TV . The reported return comes after the United States Africa Command (AFRICOM) withdrew personnel from the installation over a deteriorating runway that would have cost tens of millions of dollars to repair — raising fresh questions about the costs of America’s prolonged military involvement in Somalia, according to Stars and Stripes . “AFRICOM is aware of recent reporting that a private company has signed a contract to operate at Baledogle Military Airfield,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told the Daily Caller News Foundation in a statement. “AFRICOM is not connected to this contract and has no intent to return to Baledogle Military Airfield at this time,” the spokesperson added. “We maintain the ability to reposition forces when and where needed to conduct CT [counterterrorism] operations alongside partner forces.” Americans returned to the base in recent days, Somalia Today reported Wednesday. Additionally, the Army has been reporting Danab special forces personnel, who are traditionally trained by Americans. Baledogle Airbase is a key hub for the Danab special forces in the fight against al-Shabab, according to Kaab TV. Bancroft Global Development did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. “The relocation from Baledogle was 100% an economic decision,” AFRICOM Commander Lieutenant General John Brennan said to Stars and Stripes during a press briefing. “The surface of the airfield was declining to the point where it was becoming dangerous to land aircraft there.” The reported return occurs at a time when the once waning American presence in East Africa has begun to once again strengthen. The U.S. decided to fund the U.N. Mission to Somalia for another year, despite initially opting to withdraw funding. Additionally, Brennan recently visited Mozambique for high-level security talks, telling Stars and Stripes that there are plans to expand American military cooperation in the region. At the same time, Mozambique struggles with an ISIS insurgency that Brennan claims poses a major risk to shipping and major international energy investments, including putting the assets of large companies such as ExxonMobil in jeopardy. “With ISIS Mozambique in particular, you’re seeing an increase in their maritime capacity,” Brennan told Stars and Stripes. He urged the country to host more American-led training exercises and cut bureaucracy hindering special forces from conducting operations. The contractor alleged by Kaab TV to be involved in air base construction is not without controversy. In the past, Bancroft would not be paid by Washington, but instead be paid by foreign governments, including Uganda, Somalia and Burundi, a 2015 Foreign Policy investigation into the training of Danab special forces revealed . “We have nothing to do with the Americans,” one Bancroft employee told Foreign Policy. “We’re in charge of training Danab. We have nothing to do with the Americans, and the Americans have nothing to do with us.” Bancroft’s global director claimed that they had no contracts with the American government, and this training was part of a larger deal with Uganda. However, others believe this payment structure allows Washington a degree of plausible deniability. “Basically, it’s a way for the [United States] to avoid having to look too hard at what Bancroft or any other contractor is up to,” a U.N. official told Foreign Policy. “If everything was kosher, there would be no need to go through such maneuvers.” This investigation followed a 2013 report that Bancroft personnel worked in or near active conflict zones and were armed, despite this going against guidance, according to the United Nations . The U.N. working group behind the report warned that training could lead to direct participation in conflict. Bancroft personnel still accompany Somalian and Ugandan soldiers near the front line, per Military Africa . Additionally, Bancroft has fallen under scrutiny due to the results of several audits, including one by the Department of State Office of the Inspector General (OIG). Mission in Somalia and discussions of enhanced military cooperation in the region, particularly in response to rising threats from groups like ISIS in Mozambique. The move is expected to further enhance Somalia’s participation in regional integration efforts by making travel within the East African Community more convenient and supporting closer economic and institutional cooperation among member states. The proposed committees are expected to serve as institutional mechanisms through which both governments can identify areas of mutual interest, coordinate joint initiatives and monitor the implementation of bilateral agreements. The discussions underscored the importance of moving beyond diplomatic commitments to ensure that existing agreements and memorandums of understanding deliver practical benefits to the people of both countries. Both officials reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation and advancing concrete initiatives aimed at deepening diplomatic, economic and institutional ties. Somalia and India have maintained diplomatic relations for decades, with their partnership encompassing development cooperation, education, trade and capacity-building. The latest engagement reflects renewed efforts by both governments to give greater momentum to their longstanding relationship through stronger institutional coordination and the implementation of practical cooperation programmes. somalia.content: Radio Ergo Weekly Feedback Report, Issued: 27 Nov 2026 - Somalia | ReliefWeb Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Somalia Radio Ergo Weekly Feedback Report, Issued: 27 Nov 2026 Format News and Press Release Source Radio Ergo Posted 27 Nov 2026 Originally published 27 Nov 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 386.24 KB) Brief Summary Commentary on rainfall and its positive impact on lives and livelihoods continued to form the bulk of the calls to Radio Ergo’s nationwide feedback platform in the week 19-25 November 2026. These calls came mostly from Jubbaland, South West, Hirshabelle, and some from Galmudug. However, some callers mainly in southern locations noted a tailing off of the rainfall, patchy areas without rain, and also intensely hot temperatures. A few in Gedo and Bay regions said they were now running short of water again. Drought conditions were cited in Bari. Several callers complained about influxes of mosquitoes and rising malaria cases, and wanted mosquito control measures. In Gedo region a number of IDP callers complained of hardships and their need for aid. The following summarises the calls by theme. Health – callers in Awdhegle in Lower Shabelle and Adado in Galgadud spoke of influxes of mosquitoes in their areas and a rise in malaria and wanted the menace to be brought under control. A caller in Gedo said the mosquitoes were causing illness with headaches and fever. A caller in Bardera said they had good rainfall, but mosquitoes were their main concern. A caller in Dollow also cited a mosquito influx, adding that despite the rain people were impoverished and aid agencies hadn’t visited the area for six months. IDPs – a caller in Iftin camp, Bardera, said they and their farms were doing well after the rain. On the other hand, a female caller in Bardera identifying as an IDP said they had received little rainfall, their crops had been attacked by pests and disease, and the schools had been shut for the past six months depriving the children of education. In Qurdubey, a caller called twice on behalf of displaced families who had lost their livestock. He said those families with a few livestock left were able to sell them for a living, but others like them were facing hardship and challenging conditions including poor sanitation. He added an appeal for aid. Aid – a caller in Dollow complained that they had been registered by aid groups a few days ago, but had not received the cash aid they thought they were going to get. Another caller, location unspecified, wanted a resumption of the cash aid they used to get from WFP that had stopped. Food Security – a caller in Bardera said he wanted to share information about the high inflation and rising costs of basics they were facing. Locusts – a caller in Kismayo said he had a farm near the airport and was concerned about locusts. He wanted to know how the farmers could protect their crops. Climate – a caller in Baidoa, Bay region, said they’d been experiencing intense heat and wanted to know if this was because of climate change. Similarly, a caller in Bahdo, Galgadud, said recent days had been intensely hot and people wondered if it was a sign of rain to come, or of climate change. Other callers in Guriel, Dollow, and Kismayo also described intense heat in their areas. Agriculture – farmers in southern and some central areas complained of pests damaging a range of produce including potatoes, beans, sesame, sorghum, maize, lettuce and tomatoes. They wanted to talk with experts on Radio Ergo’s weekly farming programme. Livestock – a caller in Bardera said his camels had dukan (trypanosomiasis) and the medicine he was injecting them with was not working. He wanted veterinary advice. Several herders in Jubbaland complained of foot and mouth affecting their herds. A caller in Beletweyne wanted to know more about how pre-export livestock inspections and certifications were processed in Somalia. Drought & water shortage – a caller in Rako-raho, Bari region, said they faced drought in the area and that many people had already migrated away. He added that they were in a desperate situation and needed the Puntland authority to reach them with aid. One caller in Dusamareb said they faced drought and conflict. Several in Bay region said the rain had been poor or had stopped already, with one describing the drying up of crops and grazing. A caller in Bardera said rainfall had been little and their farms were failing due to water shortages. A female caller said that odder and water shortage were affecting their livestock. Another female caller in Lower Juba said they weren’t having rainfall, the heat was intense, and their livestock were struggling. Rainfall – a female caller in Farjeni, Bari, said they had received some light rain. A caller in Harardhere, Mudug, said they were getting heavy rain and doing well. In Galgadud, callers spoke of decent rain in Bahdo, Guriel, Abudwak, and Adado, with several noting intense heat. In Hiran, callers in Buleburte, Af-ad, and El-gal noted good rain and conditions for their livestock and farms. Callers in Baidoa, Burhakaba, and Dinsor in Bay region cited beneficial rain. One in Bakool said the rain was short-lived and they hoped for more. In Gedo, several in different districts said they had had good rain but that in some places it had stopped. A caller in Tulo-banan said the rain was good, although they were poor and there were no jobs. A number of callers in Kismayo cited beneficial rainfall helping crops and livestock, while some noted dry areas nearby. Health concerns emerged as callers noted increased mosquito populations and malaria cases, prompting requests for mosquito control. football.summary: في مباراة مثيرة ضمن الدوري السوداني الممتاز، حقق فريق الأهلي مروي فوزًا مهمًا على الهلال السوداني بنتيجة 1-0. أقيمت المباراة في استاد كريمة يوم 25 نوفمبر 2026، حيث سجل الأهلي مروي هدفه الوحيد في الشوط الأول. هذا الفوز يضع الأهلي مروي في بداية قوية للموسم، بينما يسعى الهلال للدفاع عن لقبه بعد أن بدأ الموسم بخسارة غير متوقعة. في جدول الدوري، يتصدر المريخ المجموعة بعد فوزه في مباراته الأولى، بينما يحتل الأهلي مروي المركز الثاني. المباراة كانت جزءًا من الجولة الأولى من الدوري، الذي شهد افتتاحًا استثنائيًا بمشاركة ثماني فرق. يتطلع الهلال إلى تحسين أدائه في المباريات القادمة بعد تعيين مدرب جديد، بينما يستمر الأهلي مروي في تقديم أداء قوي.
